passages.title: The public library as civic infrastructure
passages.text: A city library is often described as a quiet building containing books. That description misses its civic role. A well-run library offers a shared space in which people can study, use digital services, attend talks and encounter ideas beyond their immediate experience. Unlike a commercial venue, it does not require a purchase before a visitor may remain. This matters in cities where homes are crowded and reliable internet access is uneven. Yet the value of a library cannot be measured only by visitor counts. A library that is busy because residents have nowhere else to go may be performing an important social function, but it may also reveal a shortage of other public spaces. Nor should digital collections be treated as a reason to close physical branches. Digital access expands reach; it does not automatically replace human assistance, accessible workspaces or the informal trust built through repeated encounters. The strongest library policy therefore treats physical and digital services as complementary, and evaluates success through access, usefulness and the range of people served.

passages.title: India's digital public infrastructure
passages.text: Digital public infrastructure refers to shared digital systems that allow people, businesses and public agencies to interact at scale. India's approach has combined digital identity, interoperable payment rails and consent-based data-sharing frameworks. Such systems can reduce transaction costs and make services easier to access, particularly when they are designed to work across providers. But infrastructure is not the same as inclusion. A person without a reliable device, connectivity, accessible interfaces or confidence in the system may remain excluded even when a service is technically available online. Strong governance therefore requires privacy safeguards, grievance redressal, security standards and alternatives for people who cannot use digital channels. The central policy question is not whether every service should become digital; it is how digital systems can improve public access without making essential services conditional on technology that some citizens do not possess.

passages.title: A principle for reasonable accommodation
passages.text: Assume the following principle: an institution must make a reasonable adjustment for a person with a disability where the adjustment enables meaningful participation, does not fundamentally alter the essential nature of the activity and does not impose a disproportionate burden. The institution must consider the person's actual circumstances rather than rely on a blanket rule. A request may be refused if reliable evidence shows that the proposed adjustment would remove an essential safety requirement, but convenience alone is not sufficient. The duty is one of reasonable accommodation, not an obligation to provide every requested measure regardless of cost or effect. The institution should discuss workable alternatives before refusing. Apply only this principle to the situations below; do not assume any additional legal rule.

passages.title: Congestion and the city centre
passages.text: The city council argues that introducing a congestion charge will reduce traffic in the central district. Its report notes that cities with congestion charges often experience fewer car trips in charged zones. However, the report also observes that some drivers may divert to nearby residential streets. A residents' association concludes that the charge will therefore make the entire city less safe. That conclusion is stronger than the evidence supports: the report describes a possible displacement effect but does not establish its scale, nor does it compare the risks of diverted traffic with the risks of existing congestion. A sound assessment would measure traffic across the wider area and examine pedestrian safety, public transport use and changes in travel behaviour before drawing a city-wide conclusion.

passages.title: A community transport survey
passages.text: A neighbourhood survey recorded the main mode of travel used by 800 respondents. Forty per cent usually travelled by bus, 25 per cent by metro, 20 per cent by two-wheeler and the remaining respondents walked or cycled. Of the bus users, one quarter said they would shift to metro if service frequency improved. The survey also found that 60 per cent of all respondents travelled at least five days each week. Treat the figures as exact for the questions below.

passages.title: The case for slow journalism
passages.text: In an information environment built around speed, slow journalism asks readers to value verification, context and explanation. A breaking update can tell the public what has happened; a carefully reported account can explain why it happened, whose interests are affected and what remains uncertain. This does not mean that journalists should ignore urgency. During a disaster, timely warnings can save lives. The distinction is between speed as a tool and speed as the sole measure of quality. News organisations face commercial pressure to publish first, because attention is scarce and audience habits reward immediacy. Yet an early report that later requires substantial correction can damage trust. Slow journalism is not simply long-form writing; it is a method that makes room for checking evidence, hearing competing perspectives and acknowledging limits. Its success should be judged not by how slowly it publishes, but by whether it helps readers form a more accurate understanding.

passages.title: Climate adaptation and urban resilience
passages.text: Climate adaptation concerns adjustments that reduce harm from actual or expected climate impacts. In cities, this may include restoring wetlands, improving drainage, protecting heat-vulnerable residents and designing buildings for higher temperatures. Adaptation differs from mitigation: mitigation addresses the causes of climate change by reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing carbon sinks, while adaptation manages consequences. The two approaches are connected. For example, urban trees can provide shade and reduce cooling demand, while also improving local air quality. However, adaptation projects can create new inequalities if benefits flow mainly to wealthier neighbourhoods or if informal settlements are displaced in the name of resilience. Effective planning therefore combines scientific risk assessment with local participation, transparent funding and safeguards for vulnerable communities.

passages.title: A principle for protection of confidential information
passages.text: Assume this principle: information received in confidence for a defined purpose must not be disclosed to another person unless the information provider consents, disclosure is required by law, or disclosure is reasonably necessary to prevent a serious and imminent harm. A person relying on the harm exception must have reasonable grounds for believing the danger is serious and imminent, and should disclose only the information necessary to address it. Mere curiosity, commercial advantage or speculative concern is insufficient. Where possible, the person should first seek consent or use a less intrusive way to prevent the harm. Apply only this principle to the situations below.

passages.title: Remote work and productivity
passages.text: A company found that teams allowed to work remotely completed more tasks per employee during a three-month trial. Management concluded that remote work caused the increase. But the trial coincided with a period in which the company postponed several complex projects and introduced new task-management software. Either change could have affected the measured output. In addition, employees volunteered for the trial, so participants may have been more motivated than those who remained on site. The result is evidence worth investigating, but it does not isolate the effect of remote work. A stronger study would compare similar teams, account for task complexity and examine quality as well as quantity.

passages.title: Scholarship allocation
passages.text: A foundation has a budget of ₹18,00,000 for scholarships. It allocates 40 per cent to science students, 35 per cent to humanities students and the balance to commerce students. Each scholarship is worth ₹30,000. Assume the entire budget is distributed and every scholarship has the same value.
